analysis.investment_thesis: Aadhar Housing Finance is a focused affordable-housing lender with a 16.1% revenue CAGR and a remarkable 33.4% net profit CAGR over six years, operating in a government-tailwind segment serving LMI borrowers in Tier 2/3 cities. At P/E 20.8x and forward P/E 16.2x, the price is fair but not compelling enough for me to deploy serious capital given a ROCE of only 11.4%.
key_strengths: Net profit compounding at 33.4% CAGR (2019–2025), demonstrating improving spreads and operating leverage
Blackstone-backed promoter (64.9% holding) brings institutional governance and balance-sheet discipline
Niche LMI affordable-housing focus benefits from PMAY subsidies, reducing competitive intensity from large banks
key_risks: ROCE of 11.4% is below my 15% minimum threshold — lending economics constrain the compounding power
LMI borrower credit quality is procyclical; a job-loss or income-shock cycle would spike NPAs
Loan book funded by debt (D/E 2.55x); rising interest rates squeeze NIMs meaningfully
red_flags: ROCE at 11.4% fails my 15% hurdle — not a high-return business intrinsically
Negative operating cash flow every single year (nature of a growing HFC, but requires constant equity raises to sustain growth)
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Aadhar is a competent, narrowly focused affordable housing lender growing its loan book briskly. Net profit grew from ₹162 Cr to ₹912 Cr in six years; that is genuine compounding. The equity base nearly doubled in FY25 (₹4,450 → ₹6,894 Cr), reflecting a capital raise that will dilute per-share returns near-term but supports loan-book growth into the ₹25,000 Cr asset base.

The business does not possess a strong moat — HFCs compete on cost of funds and distribution reach, both replicable. ROCE of 11.4% tells me capital is not deployed with unusual efficiency. I would wait for a lower price (P/B closer to 2x) before adding this to a portfolio, but it is not a business I would sell if already held.
